title: His Parents Left Nellore in 1999. Their Son Just Beat the Seventh Seed at the French Open.
excerpt: Nishesh Basavareddy, a 21-year-old Indian-American wildcard from Carmel, Indiana, stunned Taylor Fritz at Roland Garros in the biggest upset of Day One.
body:
Muralikrishna Basavareddy and Sai Prasanna left Nellore, Andhra Pradesh, for the United States in 1999. They lived in San Francisco, then Irvine, California, where Muralikrishna worked at Toyota. When the company transferred him to Indiana, the family settled in Carmel, a suburb of Indianapolis better known for its corn and soybean fields than for producing tennis players.

On Sunday, their younger son Nishesh, ranked 148th in the world, walked onto Court Suzanne-Lenglen at Roland Garros and beat the seventh seed.

## Four Sets Against Taylor Fritz

Nishesh Basavareddy defeated Taylor Fritz 7-6 (7-5), 7-6 (7-5), 6-7 (9-11), 6-1 in the first round of the 2026 French Open. It was the biggest win of his career, his first victory over a top-10 player, and only his second main draw singles win at any tournament.

He entered through a US French Open wildcard programme. He was making his main draw debut at Roland Garros.

The first two sets were defined by tiebreaks in which Basavareddy held his nerve against a player with fifty times his prize money earnings and a hundred times his ranking pedigree. Fritz, the American number one, found himself unable to solve the younger man's variety — a relentless mix of drop shots, angled returns, and baseline rallies that changed tempo at will.

Fritz clawed back the third set in a marathon tiebreak that went to 11-9, but Basavareddy responded with the kind of composure that belies a 21-year-old playing on the biggest stage of his career. He took the fourth set 6-1, closing out the match with authority.

"This is easily the best win of my life," he said simply afterward.

## From Nellore to Newport Beach to Carmel

The Basavareddy family's story is a familiar one in the Indian diaspora: parents who emigrated, worked demanding jobs, and invested in their children's futures. What is less familiar is the sport they chose.

Tennis is not cricket. It does not carry the cultural weight or community infrastructure that channels generations of Indian-origin children toward established pathways. For the Basavareddy family, it started with the father playing recreationally in Irvine.

"My dad used to play for fun," Nishesh told Indian Tennis Daily. "My brother started playing a little bit then. I started playing at the local club."

When the family moved to Indiana, Nishesh was eight. He found a coach named Bryan Smith, who has guided him ever since. He also found a mentor in Rajeev Ram, the doubles world number one who happens to live in the same town — an improbable coincidence in a suburb of one hundred thousand people.

"I think I have a pretty special one here," Smith told Ram when the boy was eight. "It's incredible what he can do."

## The Rise Through the Ranks

Basavareddy was a standout junior — ranked third in the world by the ITF, winner of the boys' doubles title at the 2022 US Open. He attended Stanford for two years before turning professional in late 2024, when a hot streak of twenty-eight wins in thirty-four Challenger matches catapulted him into the Next Gen ATP Finals.

At the 2025 Australian Open, he took a set off his idol Novak Djokovic. He reached a career-high ranking of 99 in June 2025. But injuries and the grind of the tour saw him slip back to 148 by the time the 2026 clay season arrived.

The French Open wildcard was a lifeline. He used it to make history: the first American man to beat a top-10 opponent at Roland Garros since 2000.

## Why NRIs Should Pay Attention

Indian-origin athletes have made their mark in individual sports before — from Vijay Amritraj in tennis to more recent figures in golf, squash, and badminton. But Basavareddy's story hits differently for the diaspora because of the specificity of its details.

His parents are from a mid-sized city in Andhra Pradesh. They moved to a midwestern American suburb. Their son found tennis through his father's recreational hobby, was mentored by another Indian-American player from the same town, and turned a Stanford education into a professional career.

He did not emerge from an academy system. He did not have the backing of a national federation. He is not representing India. He is an American of Indian heritage, and his path to Roland Garros was built on the quiet accumulation of immigrant advantage: education, stability, and the freedom to let a child pursue an unusual dream.

Basavareddy eventually fell in the second round, but the upset over Fritz will resonate beyond one match. At twenty-one, with a top-10 scalp on clay and the full weight of a Grand Slam debut behind him, he is a name the tennis world — and the Indian diaspora — will be watching for years to come.
author: Diaspora Desk
